title: The Agentic Loop — the one concept everything hangs on

questions.prompt: Mid-task, Claude Code shows: `Run npm test? [y/n]`. Which step of the loop is this?
options: Read state — it is looking at the conversation
Act, having picked "run a command" — the permission prompt is part of the act
Observe — it is waiting for the result
questions.explanation: The tool already chose to run a command, and the permission prompt is the gate on that act. Option B is the tempting confusion, and it is a real distinction: a question about the task is decide-picked-ask, but a prompt for one specific command is act-picked-run. Option A and D name steps that produce no prompt of this kind.

questions.prompt: You ask Claude Code to find a database password in the codebase. It replies that it cannot, and says why. Which move is this?
questions.explanation: Stopping with a stated reason is one of the four moves the decide step can pick, so a reasoned refusal is the loop working as designed. Option A names a step that only reads input. Option C mistakes a deliberate stop for a fault. Option D treats a grounded explanation as invented output, which is the opposite of what a reason-stated stop is.

questions.prompt: You switch the model powering the session to a different one. Which statement is true?
options: The agent changed; the model is the loop
The model changed; the agent — the read/decide/act/observe loop that wraps it — is the same
Neither changed; the model picks moves and the agent types them out
questions.explanation: The model is the decide step; the agent is the loop around it, so swapping the model swaps one step, not the loop. Option A reverses the two. Option C collapses a distinction later lessons lean on. Option D gets the roles backwards — the loop executes moves, the model picks them.

questions.prompt: A single-turn task feels slow, and the input is not especially large. Where is the time most likely going?
options: Act — the tool call itself usually dominates wall time
questions.explanation: For a normal turn the tool call is the biggest chunk of wall time, which is why naming the slow step is the start of predicting pace. Option A is the other real possibility, but it is the one that shows up when the input is large — which the question rules out. Option C and D are not the loop steps that dominate.
